cues.text: Welcome to the Reproduction problem solving workshop.
Let n represent one chromosome set, and C the DNA amount in one unreplicated
haploid genome.
A diploid cell before DNA replication is two n and two C.
After replication, it is still two n, but four C, because each chromosome has
two sister chromatids.
After the first meiotic division, each daughter cell is n and two C.
After the second division, each product is n and one C.
These are counts per cell or nucleus, not totals pooled across all products.
Chromosome number uses centromeres; specify the stage before counting
chromatids as independent chromosomes.
In a typical flowering plant anther, a diploid microspore mother cell
undergoes
meiosis to produce four haploid microspores.
If the species has twenty four chromosomes in its diploid cells, each
microspore receives twelve chromosomes.
Ten mother cells can therefore produce forty microspores, assuming normal
meiosis and survival of every product.
Microspores are not yet sperm cells: each develops into the male gametophyte,
the pollen grain.
Separate the meiotic production of spores from the later mitotic production of
gametophyte cells and male gametes.
A question may count starting mother cells, pollen grains or sperm cells;
label
the requested object before multiplying.
A typical developing microspore divides mitotically to form a vegetative cell
and a generative cell.
At this two celled stage, the pollen grain is already a reduced male
gametophyte.
The generative cell later divides by mitosis to form two male gametes.
Some species release pollen at the two celled stage, while others release it
after the generative division.
The sperm chromosome set remains haploid because this is mitosis within the
haploid generation.
The vegetative cell supports pollen tube development; it does not become the
embryo.
Do not call every pollen grain a single male gamete, and do not assume that
three celled pollen has three sperm.
Use the typical monosporic, Polygonum type embryo sac unless the question
states another pattern.
A megaspore mother cell undergoes meiosis, usually leaving one functional
haploid megaspore while three degenerate.
Three mitotic divisions of the functional megaspore produce eight nuclei.
Organisation gives an egg, two synergids, three antipodals and a central
cell containing two polar nuclei before their fusion.
That is seven cells but eight nuclei.
If the polar nuclei have already fused, the nuclear count changes, so read the
specified stage.
The usual egg apparatus consists of the egg and the two synergids.
Do not apply this typical developmental pattern to every angiosperm without
qualification.
In the typical embryo sac, one sperm fuses with the haploid egg to form a
diploid zygote.
The second sperm fuses with the two haploid polar nuclei, or their fused
diploid secondary nucleus, to form a triploid primary endosperm nucleus.
Together these events constitute double fertilisation.
The zygote develops into the embryo, while endosperm development supplies
nutritive tissue.
If the diploid chromosome number is twenty four, the embryo has twenty four
chromosomes and the typical endosperm nucleus thirty six.
These ploidies follow the stated conventional embryo sac model.
Double fertilisation is not the fusion of both sperm with the same egg.
A seed contains tissues with different developmental origins.
In the ordinary sexual model, the embryo is a new diploid generation with
contributions from both parents.
Typical endosperm is triploid, while the seed coat develops from the maternal
ovule integuments and remains maternal diploid tissue.
The ovule develops into the seed, and the ovary usually develops into the
fruit, though accessory tissues contribute in some fruits.
Persistent nucellus is called perisperm; it is not another name for endosperm.
The endosperm can persist in the mature seed or be largely consumed during
embryo development.
State both tissue identity and origin before assigning a chromosome number.
Pollination transfers pollen to the stigma; it is not itself gamete fusion.
Autogamy occurs within a flower.
Geitonogamy transfers pollen between flowers on the same plant and is
genetically self pollination, although it needs a transfer mechanism.
Xenogamy transfers pollen between different plants of the same species.
For a controlled cross using a suitable bisexual flower, removing anthers
before pollen release helps prevent that flower supplying its own pollen.
Bagging protects against unwanted pollen, and selected compatible pollen is
applied when the stigma is receptive.
Emasculation is unnecessary for a female flower that has no anthers.
Label the controls before interpreting offspring or claiming that a transfer
produced successful fertilisation.
Finish with a model counting problem.
Suppose eighty ovules each undergo normal double fertilisation and every
resulting seed survives.
Each ovule needs one pollen tube delivering two sperm, so the minimum is
eighty
successful pollen grains and one hundred sixty sperm.
If every microspore survives and every pollen grain succeeds, twenty
microspore
mother cells can provide those eighty pollen grains.
Real pollen production is usually much larger because transfer, compatibility
and survival are not perfect.
The minimum is a consequence of the ideal assumptions, not a prediction of
field seed set.
Likewise, the number of fertilised ovules need not equal the final number of
mature seeds if some abort.
